item.title: Reported attacks on ships near Strait of Hormuz hit a new weekly high
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
What to know about the Iran war today: The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) monitoring agency said at least ten vessels have been attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz since last Sunday, a weekly high since war broke out in February, and 23 attacks were recorded since the start of the month, almost double the average.Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian denied Friday that Tehran sought nuclear weapons, expressed readiness for dialogue and condemned U.S. sanctions during talks with Georgia's prime minister.The Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. leaves the Middle East, a spokesman for Iran 's army said Friday. "If it does not leave, we will expel it," Mohammad Akraminia wrote on X . Iranian foreign minister meets with several Middle East counterparts at regional gathering Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, one of the leading members of past negotiations with the United States, met with a handful of his counterparts on Saturday at a gathering of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in Baghdad. Among those he met was Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan even as Turkey is part of a trilateral cooperation agreement with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, which is coming under fire from the Iran-backed Houthi militia. The two sides discussed "the latest developments in Palestine and Yemen, emphasizing diplomatic efforts to reduce tensions," according to the Iranian government. "During the bilateral talks, FM Araghchi also reviewed the latest developments in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, briefing his Turkish counterpart on ongoing diplomatic trends and emphasizing Islamic cooperation to face shared regional challenges," the Iranian government said on X . Araghchi also met with foreign leaders from Egypt, which said Saturday it would defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks; Libya; Lebanon; and Algeria. Saudi strikes on Yemen kill 12, Iran-backed Houthis say Saudi strikes that began overnight have killed at least 12 people in Yemen, three of them children, Houthi media reported on Saturday. Saudi warplanes targeted "civilian homes" in Taiz governorate on Saturday, killing nine people and wounding 16, the Iran-backed group's news agency said, adding people were still trapped under the rubble. The agency had earlier reported overnight strikes in Dhamar province that killed three children and wounded 17 other people. It said the strikes were carried out "using cluster bombs, which are banned internationally." The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis has launched daily raids in Yemen backing the internationally recognized government in the country's long-running civil war. Saudis intercept 4 drones over country in recent hours The Saudi-led coalition fighting against the Iran-backed Houthis have intercepted four drones over Saudi territory in the last few hours, the group said. The drones were intercepted over the capital city of Riyadh, and in the Eastern, and Southern regions, according to the coalition. The Houthis have regularly launched drones and missiles at the Saudis every day for the last several weeks. The coalition announced overnight it had taken out two missile-launch platforms in the Saada Governorate, which is the northern-most region in Yemen and controlled by the Houthis. A missile launch one week ago hit King Khallid International Airport in Riyadh and killed 13 people. President Sisi says Egypt ready to defend Saudi Arabia "if requested" Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Saturday said Egypt was ready to defend Saudi Arabia "if requested," as fighting flares between the kingdom and Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen. Since Yemen's war reignited in July, the Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi targets, including energy facilities and Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, where 13 people were killed in a single attack last Saturday. The Houthis have also blockaded the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Saudi-flagged tankers, piling pressure on energy exports as Iran presses its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz. Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian military academy, Sisi said Egypt was "not looking for a role to play" in regional conflicts, but added it was "inconceivable" for Cairo to stand by while Saudi Arabia was "harmed or its security and stability threatened." "Egypt, of course, with the directives of His Majesty King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, will carry out any measure to protect you or defend you," he said. He added any deployment would require parliamentary approval and said he hoped lawmakers would convene in an emergency session to grant authorization "if it is requested of us." "I'm not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone," Sisi said. "We are speaking only about defense." Yemen's Houthis free 159 pro-government fighters under amnesty Yemen's Houthis on Saturday announced the release of 159 pro-government fighters under an amnesty announced after they seized swathes of land in a major offensive last month. The prisoners had "voluntarily surrendered themselves without fighting" as the Iran-backed group captured strategic positions along the Red Sea, Houthi official Abdelqader al-Murtada told a press conference in Sanaa. The Houthis' war with the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government reignited in July after four years of calm, triggering attacks on Saudi oil shipments and other targets including airports. The International Committee of the Red Cross confirmed the unilateral release of 159 prisoners and said it had given support by organizing interviews and health checks, contacting families and helping arrange transport. Murtada said 323 prisoners were released under the amnesty last month after surrendering in Hodeidah governorate. Iran backs "political process" to resolve Saudi-Houthi conflict, foreign minister says Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Saturday that Tehran supports a "political process" to resolve the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis. The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi targets, including energy facilities and Riyadh's international airport, where 13 people were killed in a major attack one week ago. "We support an inclusive and comprehensive political process as the only practical and sustainable way to resolve the issue," Araghchi said in a speech at the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in Baghdad. Araghchi repeated Iran's offer to mediate between the two sides. Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh previously said Riyadh has not responded to Iran's overture. On Friday, Iran denied having anything to do with the Houthi attacks, after Saudi Arabia accused Tehran of encouraging the group's escalation. In his speech, Araghchi also said "either we build security together, or we will endure insecurity together," adding Tehran was willing "to cooperate with all its brothers and neighbours to achieve the first option." The Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon are part of Iran's "Axis of Resistance" against Israel and the United States, which also includes armed groups in Iraq. Oil tanker reportedly hits mine in Strait of Hormuz Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps on Saturday said an oil tanker was on fire in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine in the waterway at the heart of the Middle East war. "A supertanker in violation of regulations, carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil and attempting to pass illegally through the Strait of Hormuz, struck a mine, triggering an explosion and a fierce fire," the Iranian military said. The statement did not specify the exact location of the incident. "The tanker attempted to cross the strait with U.S. support... by deactivating all its tracking systems," the Guards added, also posting a video of a vessel in flames during the night. Ship attacked by RPG fired from small boat, British maritime agency said The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) monitoring agency reported on Saturday a second attack on a ship off the coast of Saudi Arabia, which took place a day early. In a post on social media , the UKMTO said: "The master of a tanker has reported being attacked by an RPG (rocket-propelled grenade) from a small boat, resulting in damage to the aft port quarter." Friday's attack is the second reported by the agency on that day off the coast of Al Jubayl in Saudi Arabia. "Crew are accounted for and reported safe," the UKMTO said, but the full extent of the damage and environmental impact were not known at the time of the report. Ship struck by "unknown projectile" off the coast of Saudi Arabia, maritime agency says A British maritime agency said Saturday it had received a report of a vessel struck on the Persian Gulf on Friday. The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said the tanker had been struck by an "unknown projectile" off the coast of Saudi Arabia. "All crew are reported safe and have been evacuated. There is no reported environmental impact at the time of report," the statement added. The UKMTO had previously reported that October had become the busiest month for reported attacks on ships in the Strait Hormuz. Reported shipping attacks jump in Strait of Hormuz, British monitor says A British monitor says October has become the busiest month for reported attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz since March, during the Iran war's opening months. That's as the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said it was "struggling to accurately report" the true number of attacks since most ships now refuse to report them. Still, UKMTO said 10 attacks were reported in the week ending Friday. One ship sank. Since early July, most attacks have occurred off Oman, where the U.S. military has been guiding vessels at risk of Iranian attack. There has been an uptick in attacks since President Trump late last month rejected a Tehran proposal to end the war and open the strait, though indirect negotiations have continued. 2 missiles strike airport in Yemen's port city of Aden, officials say Two missiles struck the airport in Yemen's port city of Aden on Friday night, police said, blaming Iran-backed Houthi rebels for the second such attack in less than a week. Police said no casualties were reported as fighting escalates in the latest front in the Iran war, one in which the rebels have attacked both neighboring Saudi Arabia and Yemen's internationally recognized government that's backed by the kingdom. A security official and a traffic controller told The Associated Press an area of the Aden airport that hosts a military unit aligned with the Saudi-backed government was hit. Both spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. There was no immediate claim of responsibility. Iran denies Saudi accusation of involvement in Houthi attacks Iran's foreign ministry on Friday rejected Saudi Arabia's accusation that Tehran was involved in Houthi attacks on the kingdom, offering to mediate between the two sides. "The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations," Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in a statement, reiterating Tehran's offer to act as a bridge between the Houthis and Riyadh. Regardless of how involved Iran has been in Houthi attacks, the two groups have long held close ties . They were once a relatively marginal group within what Iran calls its Axis of Resistance — a loose alliance of anti-Israel, anti-U.S. militant groups that includes Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon. "The Houthis are the most powerful proxy within the Iranian network, hands down," said Mohammed Al-Basha, founder of the Basha Report, a U.S.-based risk advisory group. "Any U.S. military strategy planning a campaign on Iran will have to take into consideration what the Houthis will do next." Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have killed about 20 people in the last several weeks, including 13 in one strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport last weekend. CBS/AFP Iran's president denies nuclear ambitions, says country ready for talks Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian denied Friday that Tehran sought nuclear weapons, expressed readiness for dialogue and condemned U.S. sanctions during talks with Georgia's prime minister. In his meeting with Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Pezeshkian also called for closer ties with Georgia, weeks after Tbilisi cut aviation links between the two countries following U.S. sanctions targeting Iranian airlines. The two met on the sidelines of a U.N. biodiversity summit in Armenia's capital, Yerevan. "Iran is not seeking nuclear weapons, and we consider the malicious propaganda against our country to be lies," Pezeshkian said, according to a statement from his office. "We have always been ready for dialogue. They think they can force us to surrender, but we will not bow to coercion," he added, calling U.S. sanctions against Tehran "unjustifiable and inhumane." Georgia's Civil Aviation Agency said in September it would comply with U.S. sanctions, while Kobakhidze insisted Tbilisi was not imposing its own bilateral sanctions on Tehran. Saudi-hosted Asian Cup soccer tournament remains on schedule despite Houthi attacks Asian Cup organizers insisted Friday the continental soccer championship set to be held in Saudi Arabia in early 2027 remains on track despite a wave of missile and drone attacks on the host country in recent days. The Saudi organizing committee issued a statement Friday saying it is continuing to coordinate closely with the Asian Football Confederation. The tournament is scheduled for Jan. 7 to Feb. 5. "Preparations across all organizational and operational areas are progressing according to the approved schedule, including work on venues, facilities and supporting services," Saudi organizers said. "The focus remains on delivering a world-class tournament experience for participating teams, fans and media from across Asia, while bringing the continent together through football." South Korea's Professional Footballers' Association had earlier expressed concerns following a series of attacks on the Asian Cup host country by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels. "The continued military tensions and security instability in the Middle East are issues that can never be taken lightly," Lee Keun-ho, head of the South Korean player union, said in a statement. "The safety of our national team, as well as all players participating in the Asian Cup, is a serious concern." At least 19 people, including foreigners, have been killed in more than a week of Houthi attacks targeting the Riyadh international airport, the headquarters of Saudi oil giant Aramco and other aviation, oil and military facilities across the kingdom. Several sporting events have already been canceled or postponed in Saudi Arabia, including Netflix's Six Kings Slam tennis tournament; women's tennis' WTA Finals, which were moved to the U.S.; multiple matches for the Saudi soccer club Al-Nassr, which features Cristiano Ronaldo; and an Olympic qualifying event for BMX cycling. AP/CBS Attacks on Yemen government palace compound killed 5, officials say Attacks on the palace compound of Yemen's internationally recognized government Thursday killed at least five people and wounded more than a dozen others, government officials said. In a Facebook post late Thursday, Health Minister Qasem Buhaibeh said security guards and other employees at Maashiq palace in Yemen's southern port city of Aden were among the casualties. Aden has been the seat of Yemen's government since 2015. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attacks, saying they targeted a military operations headquarters associated with Saudi forces backing the government. Two of the missiles launched by the Houthis on Thursday struck near the headquarters of the Saudi-backed coalition forces in Aden, causing damage, a Yemeni government official said. The official, speaking on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak to the media, said Friday the missiles landed near the compound used by the coalition in Buraiqah, a neighborhood west of the palace. No senior officials were there at the time of the attack, he said. Saudi-led coalition intercepts missiles and drones Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki announced a series of interceptions in successive X posts on Friday, saying Saudi forces had destroyed a ballistic missile, two cruise missiles and three drones over Saudi Arabia or the Red Sea. In a first tweet, Al-Maliki said coalition forces intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched toward Yanbu. A second post announced the interception and destruction of two cruise missiles over the Red Sea. He then reported three drones had been intercepted and destroyed in Saudi Arabia's southern region and the Riyadh region. Iraq says Iran war has deprived it of $60 billion in oil export revenue Iraq has lost around $60 billion during the U.S.-Iran war, Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said Thursday, as the fighting has blocked or severely impeded a waterway crucial to its oil exports. OPEC member Iraq was producing about 4 million barrels of oil per day (bpd) before the conflict, and exporting about 3.5 million bpd – mostly carried by tankers out of the Persian Gulf via the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's ongoing threat to vessels that fail to seek its permission to transit the strait has forced Iraq, which lacks sufficient storage capacity, to halt most production and fall back on limited exports via Syria and Turkey, by truck and pipeline respectively. Syria is set to provide an overland oil route to bypass the strait , the head of Syrian Petroleum Co. said last week. "Iraq has suffered losses estimated at around $60 billion during the recent war between the United States and the Islamic Republic of Iran," Hussein told his Italian counterpart in Rome, according to a statement from the Iraqi foreign ministry. After a heavy drop in production, Iraqi oil exports, which provide about 90% of the country's revenues, recovered modestly last month, reaching 2.6 million barrels per day between Sept. 1 and 21, according to the oil ministry. But at the same time, Iraq's foreign currency reserves have shrunk by $20 billion and consumer prices have risen sharply, plunging it into economic crisis. CBS/AFP Norwegian teen sentenced in U.K. to 20 years in prison for plotting murder for Iran-linked gang A Norwegian teenager convicted of traveling to Britain to carry out a contract killing on behalf of an international crime gang linked to Iran was sentenced Friday to 20 years in prison. Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, was found guilty in July of conspiracy to murder for agreeing to shoot someone unknown to him for $28,000 last year. He was arrested at a hotel in Huddersfield, in northern England, with two guns and ammunition two days after arriving in the U.K. In bodycam video released by police from the early hours of March 19, 2025, Natland emerges topless from his room and mimes a shooting gesture at a firearms officer before being slammed against a wall. It remains unknown who his intended target would have been. Natland, who was working part time at a pizza restaurant at the time of his arrest, was recruited by a Swedish organized crime group known as the Foxtrot Network while he was playing a game online. The group has links to the Iranian government, according to London's counterterrorism police unit. Natland was hired by a 17-year-old known as "Generalen." A court in Norway last year convicted the teenager of attempting to "contribute to murder" and sentenced him to 14 years in custody. A 16-year-old is awaiting trial in Norway for his role in the conspiracy. CBS/AP Iranian navy says a tanker is burning in the Gulf of Oman The Iranian navy said Friday that it had identified a tanker on fire in what it called a prohibited area in the Gulf of Oman, east of the Strait of Hormuz. The navy's public relations office said in a statement that military surveillance teams "discovered and identified a violating oil tanker that had caught fire in a prohibited area." The vessel had "switched off its tracking systems and was attempting to pass through a prohibited area in the Gulf of Oman." The navy did not say how the tanker "caught fire" but added that "the consequences of uncoordinated movements along routes and in prohibited areas are the creation of insecurity and serious hazards for other vessels." At least three commercial vessels have been struck in the region in suspected Iranian attacks this week. Iran says the Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. "leaves the region" The Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. "leaves" the Middle East, an Iranian army official said Friday. "If the United States leaves the region, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen and collective security will be established with the participation of the countries of the region, and the global economy will improve," army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia wrote on X . "If it does not leave, we will expel it." He did not elaborate on whether he was calling for a withdrawal of military forces sent during the current war, all U.S. military forces across the region, or military and non-military U.S. government personnel. Though there were credible reports earlier this month of oil exports from the Persian Gulf ramping back up to near pre-war levels , Iran and the U.S. continue offering conflicting narratives, with the Trump administration insisting the Strait of Hormuz is open, but Tehran claiming it is closed to all traffic unless Iranian authorities grant permission. Greek maritime risk firm Marisks warned Thursday that ships continue to face "indiscriminate attacks," even if they turn off their tracking systems, which many ships have been doing to avoid detection. Iran president says conflict in Mideast amounts to "ecocide" Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Friday urged countries to condemn what he called "ecocide" in the Middle East caused by "wars of aggression" against his country. Pezeshkian said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had taken a significant toll on nature that extended beyond national borders and required "international solutions." "What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned," Pezeshkian said at a nature summit in Armenia that was attended by United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres. Pezeshkian decried an "atmosphere of distrust" between Iran and the U.S. in a recent interview with CBS News . "As long as they don't cease doing what they're imposing on us every day, it's difficult to trust them," he said. "Every day, they increase the sanctions against us. Every day, they threaten us. Every day, they strike us, and they don't honor what they have put in writing. So, if they engage in talks, will they actually follow through?" CBS/AFP White House prepares plans to use weapon dubbed "mother of all bombs" on Iran, sources say The White House and Pentagon have prepared plans to use a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb to hit military sites in Iran if ordered by President Trump, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News. A Pentagon official told CBS News: "The Department of War plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment." A White House spokesperson said: "We do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist. President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon." Last week, Mr. Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm elections. He also touted "productive conversations" with Iran, though he did not provide specifics. CNN first reported Thursday on the plans to use the Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, or MOAB, on Iran. Mr. Trump set a precedent for using the MOAB, also known as the "mother of all bombs," when it was used in 2017 to attack an Islamic State cave complex in Afghanistan. The bomb is the largest U.S. non-nuclear weapon, weighing upwards of 30,000 pounds at a cost of $170,000 per unit. Read more here . item.title: Trump's decision to waive Russia sanctions sparks bipartisan outrage
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's abrupt decision to waive sanctions on Russia days before they were to take effect drew outrage Saturday from members of Congress, which had overwhelmingly passed the legislation in a bipartisan display of American support for Ukraine in the war with Russia . Lawmakers from both parties blasted the executive order late Friday, the latest in a series of steps that the Republican president has taken drawing the United States closer to Russia's Vladimir Putin . Trump recently announced a diesel deal with Putin to import Russian energy in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices in the U.S. that are roiling the midterm elections on Nov. 3. “Beyond irresponsible,” said Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., on social media, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed hope that the sanctions that were supposed to take effect Sunday targeting Russian's economy could be revived. “What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?” Tillis said. “It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine.” Tillis said that if Trump wants to actually bring down energy prices, he should resolve the Iran war , which is largely blamed for the spike at the pump, and “not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin.” Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas said “Lindsey would be appalled,” referring to the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., who worked endlessly on the bill before he died this summer. The bill is known as the Lindsey Graham Russian Sanctions Act. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in a statement that “by giving the Russian economy life support, Trump’s deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier.” Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said Trump is “thumbing his nose” at Congress and “enabling Vladimir Putin to continue his war of aggression.” She urged her colleagues to take action to reverse course. Trump's actions come as Ukraine is bracing for a stark winter confronting Russia's ongoing attacks on its energy infrastructure to heat homes and keep the lights on. Zelenskyy, who has endured a rocky relationship with Trump but stayed close to the U.S. lawmakers, urged supporters to speak out on behalf of the sanctions. The next steps are highly uncertain with the House and Senate are on recess until after Election Day. Trump said he was waiving the sanctions indefinitely, citing national security concerns. It is unlikely Congress would be in a position to take any action to challenge Trump’s moves until lawmakers return to Washington. Skeptics in Congress warned Trump would not follow the law It took almost a year for Graham to persuade Trump to agree to the Russian sanctions package. It was designed to impose steep tariffs on countries that import large amounts of Russian oil and energy products and was promoted as way to halt the flow of funds fueling Putin's four-year war against Ukraine. But even as Zelenskyy had watched from the visitor gallery as the Senate advanced the package after Graham's death, skeptics in Congress warned Trump would be unlikely to follow the bill once he had signed it into law a month ago. Last week, a bipartisan group of senators urged the Trump administration to more quickly clamp down on Russia, particularly the “shadow fleet” of tankers that Moscow is using to transport oil and bypass America’s sanctions. The senators noted that the bulk of the new law's provisions were to be effective Sunday. item.title: French police clash with protesters as tens of thousands rally over cost of living
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Janis Laizans, STAMOS PROUSALIS and Yann Tessier PARIS, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Violent clashes erupted between police and protesters across France on Saturday, as hundreds of thousands of people protested against rising costs and declining public services in some of the country's most destructive unrest in years. The Interior Ministry said at least 272 people had been arrested after violent ‌incidents involving hooded individuals, including in Paris, Marseille in the south, Toulouse in the southwest, Angers in the west and Lyon in east-central France. Belgium, Portugal and Italy also faced smaller-scale protests ‌on Saturday as living costs rise in Europe, while protesters in Albania again rallied against perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards. French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would not be "intimidated" by violence, and blamed the unrest on ​the "far-left" and criminals just months before a presidential election next year. "To those who clearly want to use this violence as a 'warm-up' before the presidential election, I say clearly: We will not let ourselves be intimidated. No one will impose their political agenda through violence," he wrote in a post on X. The CGT union told Agence France-Presse news agency that 800,000 people across France had taken part in Saturday's protests. The Interior Ministry did not give an estimate, and the CGT did not respond to a Reuters request for comment. Protesters said most people had marched peacefully, and put much of the violence down to troublemakers who had set out to cause damage and ‌clash with the police. "We are fighting because the cost of living is ⁠too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions," said Lola, a 19-year-old protester in Paris. TEAR GAS, FIRE AND LOOTING In some parts of Paris, police ⁠occasionally fired tear gas rounds as they retreated in the face of mostly young protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore hoodies, masks and goggles to protect against tear gas. By late afternoon, protesters reached prominent landmarks in central Paris, including the Champs-Elysees, Concorde and La Madeleine, which had been excluded from the authorised demonstration. On Saturday evening, as the protests wound down, protesters set ablaze objects including at least one car. Some tourists at a fashionable department ​store ​near the Paris opera were seen spluttering when they were caught in clouds of tear gas, and shops nearby ​were hastily shuttered. Windows of many shops and restaurants in the capital were smashed, ‌and cars and trash cans were set on fire. In Lyon, protesters torched the tourist office. In Marseille, the mayor said the town hall had been vandalised and that additional police were being sent to the city following talks with the government. In protests partly inspired by those in France, several hundred mostly young people protested in Brussels, and some clashed with police. Belgian student groups have said they are protesting against rising education costs and reforms they fear will make higher education less accessible. In Albania, police fired what appeared to be rubber bullets at protesters during a fifth day of mass student demonstrations calling for Prime Minister Edi Rama to step down. In Portugal, tens of thousands took to the streets of Lisbon following days of unrest to protest against housing and other living costs. Housing prices in Portugal have doubled since 2017, fuelling ‌one of the worst affordability crises in Europe. In Italy, a march against high costs of living in Milan degenerated into ​disorder, with police clearing the central Cathedral square with tear gas. Police in Bologna used water cannon to try to ​disperse crowds and made seven arrests after another protest turned violent, the ANSA news agency reported. FRENCH ​POLICE RESPONSE UNDER SCRUTINY The protests in France began last month at high schools in Paris' poor northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved ‌into a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending and living standards. In Paris on ​Saturday, protesters in high-visibility vests blocked streets, recalling the ​Yellow Vest movement that marked President Emmanuel Macron's previous term in office. Macron, who urged calm on Friday, is entering the final stretch of his presidency, facing a fragmented political landscape and growing pressure over the economy. France's efforts to reduce public debt have failed to reassure investors, pushing government borrowing costs to their highest levels in over two decades. Police tactics have drawn criticism following ​injuries among demonstrators, including a teenager who lost a hand after picking up ‌a stun grenade. Lecornu said more than 900 police officers had also been injured in previous protests. The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence. item.title: U.S. deficit nears $2 trillion as government spending keeps climbing
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The US federal budget deficit for 2026 officially came in Friday at $1.992 trillion, a final tabulation to close out the government's fiscal year and another reminder of Washington's spiraling reliance on red ink. This deficit number represents about 6% of the US gross domestic product and was a result of $5.403 trillion in total revenues for the fiscal year against total spending of $7.396 trillion. The 2026 reading is a 12% jump from 2025's $1.775 trillion deficit. These final numbers came in the Treasury Department's Monthly Statement for September, which covers the final month in the US government's fiscal calendar. The red ink has led to dire warnings from economists that the US now routinely runs annual deficits that were previously seen only during recessions and wars. The gross US national debt passed $40 trillion in August and now sits above $40.3 trillion. The latest "Debt to the Penny" reading from the Treasury Department came this past Wednesday, putting the gross US national debt at $40,329,229,827,541.02. A bus shelter in Washington display the US National debt in August. (Jemal Countess/Getty Images for the Peter G. Peterson Foundation) Jemal Countess via Getty Images Read more: How the soaring federal debt affects you personally The independent budget hawks at the Committee for a Responsible Budget noted in a recent analysis that "the country's future fiscal outlook is even more dismal," noting that annual deficits could reach $3.1 trillion by 2036 without a change in the fiscal trajectory. The group noted that annual interest costs on the debt are now $1.1 trillion, a record 3.4% of GDP, making it the second-largest line item in the government's budget. Interest on the debt still costs less than Social Security , but it is now more expensive than either Medicare or the defense budget. Members of President Trump's team have tried to downplay this year's tabulation — the highest annual deficit reading other than 2020 and 2021, when budgets were inflated by COVID-era spending — as a blip and insist that the US fiscal situation is getting under control. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has focused on the Supreme Court-ordered tariff refunds that have turned a revenue stream into a cost center for the government in recent months. Indeed, the impact of tariff refunds has been significant: $144.6 billion in tariff refunds were given out over the past year — but analyses of the deficit also show a variety of factors that have driven up deficits. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and President Trump are seen during an event in the Oval Office of the White House on Oct. 7. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images) Anna Moneymaker via Getty Images A Hamilton Project tracker of government expenditures shows how government spending has increased at a steady pace in 2026. The tracker looks at spending by calendar year and shows that as of Oct. 14, government spending has jumped each of the last three years. At this point in 2024 — the last year of Joe Biden's presidency — the government had spent $5.76 trillion. On Oct. 14, 2025, spending had grown to $6.13 trillion. So far this year, the government has spent $6.65 trillion. One of the drivers, a Bloomberg Government analysis found, is spending on Trump administration priorities, especially the Department of Homeland Security, whose budget is up 146% from 2025 to 2026. Revenue downturn The revenue side of the US government's budget equation has also faltered on some fronts in 2026, in part due to tax cuts implemented by Trump's "One Big Beautiful Bill." A monthly budget review from the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) released last week noted that tariff revenues declined, as did corporate income tax collections. The group calculates that corporate income taxes decreased by 16% in 2026 as the new tax cuts allowed corporations to take larger deductions "and offset the increases in those receipts that otherwise would have been expected, given the rise in corporate income." Tariffs were also a significant factor, with the Supreme Court's decision in February striking down Trump's tariffs leading to a refund process in the months that followed that has made tariffs barely a profitable undertaking for the government in 2026. The $144.6 billion in tariff refunds nearly halved the gross receipts of $317.8 billion. And at least some additional tariff refunds could be seen in the months ahead, with the government recently launching "Phase 3" of the refund process . This turnabout in tariffs led to a deficit approximately $140 billion higher than projections from just a few months ago. In February, before the tariff refunds were ordered, the CBO projected a $1.85 trillion annual deficit for this year. Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance. item.title: Trump says neither he or Musk are to blame for Ukraine drone issues
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Ukraine is still unable to use its interceptor systems against Russian drones, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday, because of speed restrictions imposed on Starshield, an upgraded military version of Elon Musk's Starlink, amid an ongoing row with President Trump. "Unfortunately, we can't use Starlink or Starshield technology on our territory today to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds," Zelenskyy said in an online group chat with reporters at the EU Summit. "They fly, and we can stop them with aircraft and other air defense, but we don't use Starlink for that, unfortunately. God willing, this will be restored." Zelenskyy said Kyiv was discussing the issue with U.S. officials, and he was told the restrictions were linked to technical issues. The Ukrainian president added, however, that Starlink appears to be operating at higher speeds on European Union territory. "Yes, we are in dialogue at the level of the military, the Ministry of Defense and diplomats, in touch with everyone including SpaceX. Nobody there is answering our military or the Ministry of Defense now," Zelenskyy said. "At various levels they say these are technical problems." "Here (in Ukraine) Starlink works up to a speed of 161 km/h, then shuts off," he continued. "In the EU it works at 180-plus and works constantly. Here it shuts off in the second minute after 161 km/h and stops working. We lose both drones and connectivity." Mr. Trump told reporters on Friday he had not limited Ukraine's access to Starlink, adding he didn't believe Musk, SpaceX's CEO, was responsible either. "Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Mr. Trump said while leaving the White House to travel for a rally in Georgia. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been." Musk said Wednesday he isn't responsible for deciding how Starshield is used, writing on X: "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances. On Saturday, Zelenskyy said Russia carried out a large attack on Ukraine's energy sector, targeting more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities across the country. A day earlier, the president said the current restrictions on Starshield had left people vulnerable to Russian drones, which was "very painful and frustrating" Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including speed limits that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions. Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent days, blaming the war between Russia and Ukraine for high global energy prices. The Trump administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel last week in an effort to ease pressure, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. In a social media post on Saturday, Zelenskyy called the move "unfortunate," adding the act, championed by late Sen. Lindsey Graham, "could have helped enormously." Later, he told journalists he believed the Trump administration will lift more sanctions on Russia. "Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I believe the 'diesel deal' is just the first step," Zelenskyy told reporters. CBS News has reached out to the White House for comment. Mr. Trump said Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire" over the weekend. Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The Russian government never confirmed it had agreed to a ceasefire. In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," urged both sides to make a deal and said the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin. "I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said. On Wednesday, Musk had tweeted : "Time for Zelensky to go." item.title: Judge threatens to sanction Trump for delaying deposition in $10 billion BBC case
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Topline A federal magistrate judge threatened Friday to levy sanctions against President Donald Trump for failing to “participate” in his own defamation lawsuit against the BBC, after the broadcaster informed the court that Trump had backed out of a planned deposition in the case and suggested he couldn’t be interviewed until next year. President Donald Trump walks on the South Lawn as he departs the White House on October 12 in Washington, DC. Getty Images Key Facts Magistrate Judge Enjolique A. Lett issued an order Friday directing Trump to file a response to the BBC regarding his deposition by Oct. 22, noting the court had already “admonished” the president for his “lack of participation” in the case “to no avail.” Failing to “strict[ly]” comply with the court’s schedule for discovery in the case, Lett wrote Friday, “will lead to sanctions.” Trump has sued the BBC for $10 billion, claiming the broadcaster allegedly defamed him by “deceptively” editing a video of the president’s speech on Jan. 6, 2021 for a 2024 documentary, in order to falsely suggest Trump was trying to incite violence on Jan. 6 and bias viewers against him in the 2024 election. As part of discovery in the lawsuit—where both sides gather evidence to support their case—the BBC is trying to get a deposition from Trump, which it said in a filing Tuesday was supposed to take place Friday. After first failing to coordinate with the BBC about the logistics for the deposition, Trump’s lawyers told the broadcaster the president wouldn’t be able to attend the deposition because of “other matters of national importance,” and wouldn’t be available to testify until January 2027 at the earliest—despite discovery in the case being scheduled to end in December. Trump’s legal team did not directly respond to the threat of sanctions or the BBC’s request for the court to force Trump to be deposed, but alleged in a statement to Forbes that the president’s lawsuit “is holding the BBC accountable for its defamation and reckless election interference.” What to Watch for The BBC has asked the court to compel Trump to be deposed in the case in a reasonable timeframe, and Lett agreed Friday to discuss the issue at a hearing on Oct. 22. It remains to be seen if the judge could levy any sanctions against Trump or his attorneys, and what those punishments could look like if so. Crucial Quote The BBC noted in its filing Tuesday that the court “has been required to intervene at every juncture to cajole even the most basic participation in the discovery process out of” Trump, quoting a past case that argued it’s “not the court’s role, nor that of opposing counsel, to drag a party kicking and screaming through the discovery process,” especially when Trump “was the party which filed this lawsuit” in the first place. The president “chose to file this lawsuit and, in doing so, he accepted the obligations of civil litigation,” the BBC’s attorneys argued to the court. Tangent The debate over Trump’s deposition is one of several taking place in the BBC case, as the broadcaster is also seeking testimony from Trump allies like his children Donald Trump Jr. and Ivanka Trump and son-in-law Jared Kushner. The BBC told the court in August that it had so far been blocked from serving subpoenas to the president’s family members in person because of their Secret Service protection, claiming the subpoenas were necessary because the Trump children and Kushner have “personal knowledge” of Trump’s “intention” behind his Jan. 6 speech. The court ruled in October that the broadcaster could instead serve the Trump family through alternate means—like sending a certified letter or contacting their attorneys—paving the way for those depositions to take place. The BBC was less successful in getting a deposition from former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson , who assisted Trump’s then-chief of staff Mark Meadows on Jan. 6 and has testified to Congress about the attack on the Capitol. Hutchinson asked the court to throw out her subpoena, and the court agreed , siding with Hutchinson’s argument that her testimony would be “irrelevant” and would “subject her to oppression and harassment.” Key Background Trump sued the BBC for defamation in December over its 2024 “Panorama” documentary, which aired in the U.K. before the 2024 election, but did not air in the U.S. The documentary quoted the president as telling supporters on Jan. 6, “We’re going to walk down to the Capitol... and I’ll be there with you. And we fight. We fight like hell.” In actuality, Trump said, “We’re going to walk down to the Capitol, and we’re going to cheer on our brave senators and congressmen and women.” He then made the comment to “fight like hell” more than 50 minutes later. The BBC has apologized to the president for the editing job, saying it gave “the mistaken impression that President Trump had made a direct call for violent action,” but has strongly denied it was defamatory. While Trump initially argued the BBC’s editing job had hurt his businesses, the lawsuit now only argues that it harmed his personal reputation, as the court allowed the president to narrow his lawsuit after the BBC asked Trump to turn over significant financial information about his assets and the value of his businesses. item.title: The online campaign to share the Cornell rape accuser's identity reached millions
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
As a rape investigation at Cornell University spiraled into a national firestorm, some people went online to seek the identity of the alleged victim. Social media posts on X that attempted to reveal the name of the woman at the center of the case, identified in court filings only as Jane Doe, were viewed more than 87 million times over two weeks, according to data reviewed by The Washington Post. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Facebook, Instagram and TikTok attempted to limit the spread of content purporting to identify Jane Doe. All three platforms blocked searches for an alleged name for Jane Doe, although they appeared to allow some posts containing that name to stay online. Things were different on X, the platform owned by Elon Musk. The service allowed searches for the alleged name for Jane Doe and the company's chatbot, Grok, also posted it in replies to users at least 300 times, according to data compiled by researchers at the Center for Countering Digital Harm. X posts claiming to name or identify Jane Doe received 87 million views in a two-week period after local prosecutors said on Sept. 28 that they would reopen the investigation, according to the researchers. "A responsible organization would start thinking … does this break our rules? If not, something's wrong with our rules and we need to fix them," said Imran Ahmed, the chief executive of the nonprofit, which was previously known as the Center for Countering Digital Hate. "The problem is that we have accepted a lazy untruth, which is that there is nothing we can do about these platforms, and we have no say in the way they behave," he said. X did not respond to a request for comment. The platform's privacy policy prohibits sharing some types of private information without consent, such as a person's home address. It lists others, including names and birthdates, as data that "we don't consider to be private." Since Jane Doe filed a lawsuit alleging that she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house party in 2024, she has been harassed by anonymous callers and subjected to doxing, where people attempt to reveal personal information online, according to her lawyer, Thomas Giuffra. He has also said that police appeared at her parents' home with guns drawn after a false report of an ongoing murder, a tactic known as swatting. Doe's suit seeks damages from seven fraternity members and Cornell University, among others. Several young men who share names with those accused in the lawsuit have also been targeted by harassment. Giuffra has said that online users have claimed to identify at least three women as Jane Doe on social media. The online response has been so ferocious that the judge in the case ordered several key documents, including the initial complaint, to be sealed over concerns about doxing. On X, the platform's artificial intelligence chatbot Grok contributed to the flood of posts containing alleged information about Jane Doe. Grok, which can publicly reply to users of the platform, appeared to pick up the alleged name from the online chatter. In some cases Grok provided the purported name in response to questions about Jane Doe. In others, the chatbot declined to confirm user requests to verify Jane Doe's identity and noted that alleged information for her was from unverified online speculation. When some users asked Grok to confirm their speculation about a partially redacted version of Jane Doe's signature in court documents, the chatbot obliged. "Highly probable," Grok said of one guess. "High plausibility," it responded to another. Grok's public posts in response to X users have previously caused controversy and forced a reaction from the platform. After users prompted the chatbot to digitally edit photos of women and girls into sexualized content, X said it had limited the feature. The first traces of X posts attempting to identify Jane Doe appeared on Sept. 29, the nonprofit's researchers said - the day after New York state prosecutors announced that they would reopen their investigation into the alleged rape. The posts peaked around the weekend of Oct. 3. Over the course of 10 days, more than 2,700 distinct users posted, nearly 90 percent of them with five posts or fewer. Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, said its policies do not allow content that reveals the identity of people in legal cases where that has been restricted from public disclosure. TikTok did not have a comment. Limiting the search of a specific phrase - as TikTok, Instagram and Facebook did for an alleged name of Jane Doe - doesn't prevent potentially harmful content circulating. Users still get the vast majority of their content from their algorithmic feeds, said Laura Edelson, a professor at Northeastern University. A search block creates an "endless cat-and-mouse game," said Katherine Cross, a PhD candidate and lecturer at the University of Washington Information School. Users could easily get around the restrictions by substituting other characters in for letters, or swapping the order of keywords, she said. Platforms should also take down problematic posts, Cross said in an email. "The harm is already being done, and there is something profoundly inadequate and tokenistic about the search block," she said. item.title: Trump's election fraud task force is going after the people who investigated him
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The White House task force that President Donald Trump charged with uncovering evidence of election fraud hasn’t produced any. Instead, it has shifted to releasing records that his administration is using to help build a public case against officials who investigated him. The president initially promoted the task force, led by pro-Trump journalist John Solomon, as part of a push to uncover election fraud. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. But more recently, the task force has been releasing law enforcement records from past investigations into Trump, including special counsel Robert S. Mueller III’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election and special counsel Jack Smith’s investigation into Trump’s handling of classified documents after the end of his first term in early 2021. Trump allies and some of his political appointees view those materials as useful evidence in the ongoing Florida-based grand conspiracy case - the Justice Department’s most complex and ambitious effort to indict past administration officials who investigated Trump. Even with the fanfare around the release of the files, legal experts and former law enforcement officials said the records show investigators following normal, court-authorized procedures. Still, Trump and his most ardent allies, view the task force as a win. For years, they have complained that the intelligence community has worked to undermine Trump’s presidency and concealed materials related to investigations involving him. The Solomon task force was intended to address these complaints, bypassing the usual bureaucracy by giving the conservative journalist a direct channel to Trump, who has the authority to declassify materials. Some prosecutors on the grand conspiracy case are frustrated with how long it takes to obtain intelligence files related to their investigation and perceive Solomon as better equipped to access those documents quickly, according to two people familiar with the probe who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly about the case. The investigation in Florida has been hobbled by high-profile resignations from the prosecution team and struggles to build the evidence necessary to obtain indictments. Meanwhile, the White House has for months released records in batches through the task force during background press briefings at which officials have presented the documents as evidence of wrongdoing by Trump’s adversaries. The investigation is a priority for the president, who has publicly called for the Justice Department to indict his perceived political enemies, including Obama-era officials James R. Clapper Jr., who was the director of national intelligence, and John Brennan, who led the CIA. In recent weeks, the prosecutor appointed to head the investigation, Joseph diGenova, resigned amid pressure to bring indictments quickly, according to two people familiar with the personnel matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss it publicly. Solomon said the task force is separate from the Florida probe and is not communicating or working with prosecutors. That arrangement is intended to avoid the appearance of political interference, according to the two people familiar with the probe. Solomon, in an interview, contrasted his task force’s efforts with those of the Florida prosecutors. “They’re worried about the court of law, and what the president has created here is something that can serve the court of public opinion,” he said. “They’re two different courts, they are both important, and I think both can be achieved without interfering with the other, and so far I think we’ve straddled that line.” “This could be considered an overt act and an ongoing conspiracy,” an administration official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the sensitive investigation, said of documents the White House released Sept. 9 concerning the FBI interview of then-national security adviser Michael Flynn in February 2017. “We think that’s significant and maybe at the heart of some of the things currently being investigated.” The legal theory underpinning the Florida probe is untested, and the investigation has produced many subpoenas but no indictments. Much of the investigation appears to rely on intelligence documents that date back nearly a decade, meaning the statute of limitations would normally bar the government from prosecuting any offenses involved in compiling them. But prosecutors are trying to prove that these materials were just one part of a long-running conspiracy by officials to deprive Trump of his rights, beginning with the Russia investigation during his first term and continuing through the investigation into his alleged retention of classified materials at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida. DiGenova resigned last month, and another Trump loyalist, Kurt Olsen, left the team amid disagreements over how long the investigation was taking. Trump repeatedly expressed frustration with Attorney General Pam Bondi’s failure to prosecute his opponents before firing her in April. A previous reexamination of the 2016 Russia probe by the Justice Department inspector general found no evidence of anti-Trump bias. Another, led by special counsel John Durham, accused the FBI of moving too quickly and resulted in one guilty plea from an FBI lawyer and two acquittals. The White House releases have not significantly altered the public record. The documents include notes from that era, including Flynn’s FBI interview and records of a brief investigation into then-Attorney General Jeff Sessions that Mueller’s team swiftly closed. The Flynn documents included handwritten notes and a summary of his FBI interview that led to charges of lying about a call with the Russian ambassador. (Flynn pleaded guilty but later tried to withdraw his plea, and Trump pardoned him.) The FBI’s summary was consistent with the allegations in the indictment. But the administration official said there could be discrepancies between the summary and the underlying notes. The Sessions records involved his interactions with the Russian ambassador, which got absorbed into the Mueller probe. The records showed investigators interviewed Sessions and immediately closed the file. The administration official said the investigation never should have been opened. On Friday, the task force took aim at Trump’s first impeachment by releasing State Department emails and memos between officials who testified in the House hearings. The documents involve concerns about the appearance of impropriety surrounding Hunter Biden’s work with a Ukrainian energy company, as those officials testified at the time. The task force moved to more recent history with its disclosures on Oct. 5: declassified records from the classified documents investigation in early 2023 showing the FBI monitoring calls to and from top Trump aide Susie Wiles, who is now the White House chief of staff. The monitoring, conducted with court approval and using a technique called a pen register, tracked phone numbers from Wiles’s calls but not their content. On Monday, the task force released the Smith team’s applications for court approval, which said Wiles’s calls could provide evidence of crimes such as lying or obstruction. The administration official portrayed the surveillance of Wiles as a violation of constitutional guarantees of free speech and the right to a lawyer. But Paul Cassell, a former federal judge who is now a law professor at the University of Utah, said pen registers are routine in criminal investigations. “To say this violates the Sixth Amendment would be going too far,” he said. “The questions that swirl around this really are not so much about pen registers as about whether targeting Trump and his lawyers and those who were surrounding him was legitimate.” Notwithstanding the change in focus, the task force’s documents are compiled on the White House’s website under the heading “election integrity.” Solomon, who does not have a security clearance and sees only the redacted versions of declassified documents, said that he is negotiating a dozen more releases with government agencies and expects the task force to wrap up its work in the late fall. So far, it has released 113 documents and 832 pages in 14 batches. “My goal in this is not to do anything except to be a neutral arbiter of releasing information to the public,” he said. “That would be a good epitaph on the tombstone of the project to say, hey, we learned a few things that we didn’t know.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/17/trumps-election-fraud-task-force-is-going-after-people-who-investigated-him/

item.title: Trump is hitting the campaign trail. But he's largely missing from GOP ads.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Donald Trump is barnstorming the country to boost Republicans in the final weeks of the midterms. But many candidates want to keep that support quiet. The president is nowhere to be found in GOP ads, even in red states where Republicans were happy to tout his endorsement two years ago. And some candidates are hesitant to appear with Trump on the campaign trail — even as they hope he will help juice turnout among the MAGA base in November. Democratic House and Senate candidates and outside groups have spent $145 million on general election ads mentioning Trump, while Republicans have spent just $8 million, according to a POLITICO analysis of data from AdImpact, which tracks political advertising. That's in sharp contrast to 2024, when GOP candidates spent $62 million on ads mentioning Trump. "Trump is at historic lows right now, so if he comes to your district or state, it's about getting the Republican base vote out there and that can certainly help," said Ron Bonjean, a longtime GOP strategist. "But it's really important for the candidates not to be talking about Trump 24/7 on the campaign trail." The unfavorable national political environment leaves few incentives for GOP candidates to tie themselves to Trump, and more and more Republicans in competitive races have broken with the president on issues such as the Iran war and tariffs. When Republicans do mention Trump in ads, they often aren't touting his support. In Alaska, GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan has run an ad citing how he "voted to force Trump's DOJ to release the Epstein files." The silence on the airwaves is especially stark in red states like Nebraska and Ohio. In 2024, Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.), who was facing a challenge from independent Dan Osborn, and now-Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), who was challenging then-Sen. Sherrod Brown, both ran several general election ads featuring endorsements from Trump. The president won Nebraska by more than 20 points and Ohio by 12 points that year, with Fischer and Moreno also winning their races. But this cycle, the GOP isn't focusing its ads on Trump in either state, as the match-up between Osborn and Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts heats up in Nebraska and Brown seeks to oust Republican Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio. Both Ricketts and Husted appeared at Trump rallies earlier this month. Still, Trump is absent from all Republican Senate ads in Ohio, and the only Ricketts ads that name the president accuse Osborn of disparaging Trump supporters — but don't mention Trump's endorsement. "The war in Iran, I think, has become a real noose around the neck of Republican candidates because of the affordability crisis," said former Ohio Rep. Jim Renacci. A nonprofit he works with surveyed voters on whether GOP candidates should appear with Trump and found that "in most cases you do not want [Trump] standing near you, which is why I was a little bit surprised that Jon Husted has had two events with President Trump, because I do believe there's a strong headwind in Ohio, and a big change from 2024." Husted's campaign spokesperson Amy Natoce told POLITICO in a statement, "President Trump won Ohio decisively three times by 8 points, 8 points and 11 points. If we successfully turn out the MAGA vote this November, then we will retire Sherrod Brown for good." The National Republican Senatorial Committee did not respond to a request for comment. "President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said. "The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump's winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats' extreme liberal policies and obstruction." Another Republican operative, who is based in Ohio and like others was granted anonymity to speak candidly about their own party, said GOP candidates need to find a way to talk about the Trump administration — no tax on tips, protecting social security — without mentioning the guy in the Oval Office. "This is a historically unpopular president," said the strategist, who has worked on multiple statewide races over the course of the last 15 years. "We all agree with that, and so it's kind of hard to attach yourself on the airways, I think, too closely to him." Trump's rallies, unlike candidates' ads, are seen more as targeting the president's base. He's not only visiting traditional battlegrounds like Georgia and Michigan, but also typically safe red states like Alabama and Kansas. Still, his events have been a source of tension with some GOP candidates. When Trump's team was making plans for the president to campaign in Michigan last week potentially in western Michigan, several Republican candidates and their teams up and down the ticket initially didn't know whether they should attend and be seen with the president, according to three Republicans with direct knowledge of the conversations, who were granted anonymity to share private details. They were concerned about being associated with Trump's tariffs, which have hammered the state, along with high fuel prices amid the Iran war. Trump officials scrapped the event and said the president would visit the state later in the month. Trump is now scheduled for a rally in the state on Oct. 25. "[Republican candidates] are going to do what they need to do," said one GOP pollster close to the White House. "What the White House and the president are doing is they are targeting places where they think the president can be helpful." Trump has allowed Republicans to discuss issues pertaining to their states or districts as "he understands that it is not a balk on him," said one White House official, granted anonymity to speak candidly. If Trump "was to believe that all these individuals were balking him, I A) don't think that he would want to be on the road every day, and B) I do think that you would probably see a more vocal President Donald J. Trump on Truth, et cetera, kind of voicing his opinion on it," the official said. The president and his team are giving most Senate GOP candidates especially a wide latitude to break with some of his policies at times, according to two other White House officials involved in the conversations. Trump, they said, understands the need for vulnerable candidates to create some distance, even though in the past he has lashed out at members of his party for similar moves. Republicans in the more MAGA-friendly House, however, are expected to run more in lock-step with the president. Only the most at-risk candidates are afforded some room to break with Trump, the officials said, given the tidal wave of chaos that can spur within the conference. One GOP strategist working on a battleground House race, granted anonymity to discuss private information, said he had gotten pre-approved from the White House for his candidate to miss a planned rally. Still, the strategist cautioned, that doesn't mean Trump won't berate someone from the stage when he notices the candidate is missing. Republicans still see Trump as a unique motivator for his base and rallies as a tool to help turn out voters who might be driven by the president. With Democratic voters already energized by opposing Trump, the GOP has less to lose by bringing the president out to turn out MAGA voters too. "The reality is, Democrats are going to vote in this midterm," said Paul Shumaker, a Republican strategist from North Carolina, where Trump is set to return for a rally next week as GOP Senate nominee Michael Whatley struggles to close the gap in his race. "And what Republicans need to be doing is focus on what they can do to improve their voter turnout on their side." Lauren Fedor, Myah Ward, Andrew Howard and Alex Gangitano contributed to this report. item.title: Online forum controlled by Nevada GOP House candidate contains slurs and Nazi talk
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Long before running for Congress , Marty O’Donnell was an award-winning music composer for the popular “Halo” video game franchise. His work drew legions of fans to an online forum, which the Nevada Republican has tried to turn into a galvanizing force as he tries to unseat a Democrat in a Las Vegas area district that could help decide House control . O’Donnell has served as the group’s de facto leader, referring to himself as its “benevolent dictator” while tapping its members for campaign cash and harnessing their enthusiasm in his bid. The campaign held a two-day event for forum members this month at a casino that included a video game tournament, panel discussions and speeches. There is another side, however, to what is known as “The Marty Army.” An Associated Press review of thousands of posts made on the forum between 2022 and 2026 found racial slurs, minimizations of Nazi Germany and defenses of white nationalist conspiracy theories. “It wasn’t a couple of crazies. The popular sentiment was, ‘Yes, slavery should be legal,’” said Deacon Dameron, a former group member who said O’Donnell banned him for calling another user a “dork.” Many views espoused in the forum, which is controlled by O’Donnell and his handpicked moderators, are at odds with some of the values articulated by the candidate and his campaign. For example, O’Donnell has staunchly defended Israel and condemned bigotry. In a statement, campaign spokesman Keith Schipper said O’Donnell “has zero tolerance for hate" in his forum. Since becoming aware of the issue in the spring, the campaign “dedicated a staffer to monitor” and “remove people that spew racist and antisemitic vitriol,” Schipper said. “Unfortunately, some posts have been missed over the years.” Schipper said nearly 200 users have been banned “because of hateful rhetoric, including many of the people flagged by the Associated Press. Marty’s support of Israel is unequivocal and, as seen in various interviews and online posts, he will not tolerate the rise of antisemitism in our country. Marty will continue to fight bigotry, misinformation, and hate toward Israel because it is the right and moral thing to do.” O’Donnell, who is endorsed by President Donald Trump, is running against four-term Rep. Susie Lee in the Nov. 3 election as Republicans look to hang onto their razor-thin majority. In a sign of how Republicans are triaging their chances in a tough environment, they pulled back spending this week in a handful of congressional races, including O’Donnell’s. From ‘Halo’ to emoji slurs Most of the chat group’s comments concern video games and gaming strategies. A section is reserved for questions about O’Donnell’s work on “Halo” games. After O’Donnell announced his first run for Congress in 2024, when he finished fourth in the party primary, some discussions centered around news and policy. Many of the offensive and controversial remarks came in freewheeling replies to otherwise anodyne comments about current events, politics or games. In May 2022, for example, a member wrote, “WE STAND WITH MARTY.” Others reacted to the post using letter emoji to spell out — incorrectly — a racial slur for Black people. More soon chimed in, using emoji letters to invoke another anti-Black slur. Users were likely restricted from properly spelling out such words because, by design, the platform prevents emoji from being used more than once in reaction to a post. During a January 2025 discussion concerning free speech, a forum member expressed a desire to use a racial slur but refrained because “that’s not the attention Marty wants.” Dameron, the former group member, and another former user said posters relied on coded language because more overt racist comments were likely to draw scrutiny from moderators. The other user spoke on condition of anonymity over fears of retaliation. “The Marty Army” began as a fan forum “The Marty Army” began as an inside joke. Developers of “Halo” created the chat room in 2001 on a website devoted to the game. The name they chose was meant to invoke a club for rabid fans of the glam rock band Kiss. O’Donnell joined the chat group and assumed control of the forum. He relocated it to Discord, a popular online platform. His candidate website contains a link to the Discord chat group, which he has also publicized from his account on the social media platform X. “Hey all! If you’d like to be part of my run for Congress, you can be part of Marty’s Army,” O’Donnell said in an X post after he launched his 2024 campaign. O’Donnell has stated repeatedly that users who espouse racist or antisemitic views will be banned. He also threatened, at times, to delete posts. The AP found some users who espoused Nazi sympathies were kicked off the forum, but many of their posts remain. A user suggested in March 2024 that the Nazis “did some good things” that were “completely overshadowed by the terrible things they did.” Another that month asked, “Was Hitler really an evil guy?” “Like aside from the Holocaust,” the user added, “did he really even do anything wrong?” In February, a third member posted, “Heil Hitler.” O'Donnell said he wore a Mussolini mask Current and historical fascist figures have also drawn approval. O’Donnell wrote on the forum that he rejects fascism. But he also shared a photo of himself wearing what he said was a mask of Benito Mussolini, the Italian dictator and key Hitler ally, that he wore to a Halloween party. O'Donnell's campaign denied he dressed up as Mussolini. “This mask was part of a scary Halloween costume nearly two decades ago. It was not labeled a Mussolini mask when he bought it nor was he dressed up as Mussolini for the holiday,” Schipper said. “He purchased it because it was the ugliest, creepy mask on the shelf. He jokingly referred to it as a ‘Mussolini mask’ years later because he realized it vaguely looked like Mussolini.” O’Donnell stated this year that he had been unaware of the resurgence of antisemitism. He told a conservative news outlet in September that he thought “that antisemitism is something we don’t have to worry about anymore.” “I guess it just went under the surface and it has been percolating there,” he added in the interview with the Washington Reporter, which was founded by Republican political strategists. O’Donnell made the comment after the news site Jewish Insider reported that he hosted Charles Cornish-Dale, a far-right influencer with Nazi sympathies, on his own podcast, “The Marty O’Donnell Show.” O’Donnell pledged to ban those who espouse antisemitism In the spring, O’Donnell warned users on the forum that if there was “even a hint of antisemitism” the offending member would be “instantly banned.” Users responded to his post with an emoji of an exaggerated nose and “GOY,” a sometimes disparaging Yiddish term for non-Jews. Some anti-hate groups view the use of the nose emoji as antisemitic, while goy is a term that has been appropriated by those who espouse antisemitic views. Wendy Melillo, an associate professor of journalism at American University who researches extremist chat rooms, said such comments were clearly “coded antisemitic hate speech.” Melillo said other posts she reviewed were more explicit. “There is nothing coded,” she said, “about ‘Heil Hitler.’” Some members of “The Marty Army” are aware the forum could pose a liability. In 2024, a user wrote that O’Donnell’s political career could face trouble “if someone does a vulnerability study and they find this server.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/online-forum-controlled-nevada-gop-123530042.html
