item.title: Judge denies gag order request in Cornell sex assault civil case
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A New York judge on Friday rejected a request to impose a gag order in the civil case brought by a former Cornell University student who alleged she was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house in 2024, calling the request a "'side show' meant to muddy the waters and distract from the merits of the claims and defenses involved in this case." Judge Phaedra Perry-Bond said the public statements made by Jane Doe's attorney that one of the men named in the civil lawsuit used to justify the request "express nothing more than [his] opinions." Cornell president defends response to Jane Doe allegations in heated faculty meeting "Expressing opinions on the case or reporting on how the litigation has impacted clients cannot alone serve as a factual basis for limiting an individual's First Amendment rights," Judge Perry-Bond wrote. "While the Court agrees that [he] should not make statements that certain parties spoliated evidence, especially where, as here, no discovery has yet to take place, those isolated statements, without more, are insufficient to show the serious risk of prejudice required by precedent and the United States Constitution." The judge encouraged the attorneys in the case to work together to prevent their clients from facing threats, harassment, and doxing. "The Court believes that given the notoriety of doxing related to this case, it would serve all parties' interests to work together to ensure their clients and others may be safeguarded, to the extent possible, from being inundated with threats or harassment from malicious outside actors," she wrote. Angelina Katsanis/Reuters - PHOTO: Cornell University in Ithaca, New York Perry-Bond also rebuked the lawyer who requested the gag order for including in a court filing an email exchange with an attorney for one of the other men. "The Court will not tolerate its docket being used to generate media controversy, and this Court does not tolerate attorneys, especially attorneys who are not even involved in this case, engaging in mudslinging," she wrote. The attorneys requesting the gag order had asked for "narrowly tailored restrictions" that would prevent lawyers and parties in the civil case from commenting on the allegations outside of court, arguing in their motion that a gag order would limit "possible juror prejudice" and prevent the potential release of sensitive information that could lead to " threats, doxing, intimidation, and extrajudicial contact." In a statement responding to the motion response, an attorney for Jane Doe, Thomas Giuffra, argued that the attorney for one of the men "has tried to rebut the claims in this case by engaging in a wholesale leaking of confidential documents, giving interviews calling Ms. Doe's story into question and calling her lawsuit immoral. These attempts to shift the narrative have not been successful." Accused Cornell University student asks for gag order A then-undergraduate student identified only as Jane Doe made a complaint to campus police in November 2024, three weeks after the alleged incident occurred, that she had been sexually assaulted by a group of men at the Chi Phi fraternity house. She filed a civil suit against seven men and the university alleging that she had been drugged and raped. The men denied all of the allegations. The university has said it takes allegations of allegations of sexual violence "extremely seriously" and that it "investigated and adjudicated the allegations consistent with university policies." The school said it conducted a "thorough" Title IX investigation and "issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell. This week, Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff announced that all parties and social events at fraternity houses are suspended for the rest of year while the university considers whether fraternity life can continue at the Ivy League school. "It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," Kotlikoff said Tuesday. No criminal charges have been filed, but an investigation by the New York attorney general is ongoing. The case has rocked the university and started conversations about treatment of sexual assault allegations on college campuses across the country. President Trump's embattled new press secretary Katie Zacharia was forced out Friday after less than a week on the job. Zacharia confirmed widespread reports that Trump had let her go in a post on X just after 9 p.m. ET Friday, alongside a photo of the two of them in the Oval Office. “President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man,” she wrote. “I wish more Americans appreciated him. No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to. It was an honor to work for him.” White House Communications Director Steven Cheung told CNN in a statement that Zacharia "will continue to support the President as she transitions to a new role." Zacharia is the shortest-tenured White House press secretary in U.S. history. Her five days on the job fell well short of Anthony Scaramucci’s 11 days as Trump’s communications director in 2017. Trump is unlikely to name a new press secretary anytime soon, two sources familiar with his thinking told NBC News . Earlier Friday, Trump signaled that Zacharia was on her way out, telling reporters that he had asked Zacharia to "reconsider" whether she "need[s] this." "I told her, 'I think you're better off being happy and I don't think you could ever be happy in this job,'" Trump said. Asked if he was planning to "fire" Zacharia, the president said no. But, he added, "I want her to have a good life. I don't want [her] to have a life like she's led in the last three days. She is being brutalized by the media." Around the same time, multiple outlets reported that Zacharia had already been let go. Citing "three people familiar with the matter," the New York Times reported on Friday afternoon that Trump had "fired" Zacharia. A senior White House official told Fox News that Zacharia is "transitioning out" of her role, and CBS News, Politico and the Washington Post published similar reports. Zacharia was in the middle of an interview with the Wall Street Journal at her West Wing desk shortly before 1 p.m. Friday when she was called away, the Journal reported . She had just told the reporters, “There are no staffing changes that are happening.” Senior Trump adviser Jason Miller then knocked on her door and said Vice President JD Vance wanted to talk. “JD wanted to chat with us real quick,” Miller said, according to the Journal. Zacharia left and never returned to the interview. Trump: "I told Katie that in my opinion she was treated very very unfairly by the news. Let's call it the fake news. I said, 'Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this.' We're talking about doing something. I want her to have a good life. She's being brutalized by the… pic.twitter.com/Ivkk5imCjS — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) October 16, 2026 The president announced on Friday, Oct. 9, that he had chosen Zacharia, a conservative commentator and former Department of Homeland Security spokesperson, to replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the administration in August. Zacharia started at the White House on Monday and gave her first press briefing on Tuesday. But she has spent the days since then facing questions about her own legal credentials rather than Trump's agenda. In his post on Truth Social announcing her appointment, Trump described Zacharia as an "attorney" as well as "a devoted fan and member of MAGA!" Zacharia holds both a law degree and a bachelor's degree from Pepperdine University, and her LinkedIn page says she served as "general counsel" at Fix California, a nonprofit founded by former acting Kennedy Center director Ric Grenell to promote conservative policies in the Golden State. In media appearances, Zacharia has repeatedly described herself as a lawyer. But the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that while Zacharia sat for the California bar exam after graduating from law school, she "didn't pass." A senior administration official confirmed to NBC News that Zacharia did not pass the California bar exam. Reuters also investigated her credentials and "could not find records showing Zacharia was registered as an attorney or member of the bar in any U.S. state or the District of Columbia." Asked by reporters Tuesday on the South Lawn where she passed the bar, Zacharia twice replied, "When I moved to China." In a phone interview with the New York Times on Wednesday , Zacharia said she misheard the question. "I assumed the question was, 'Where were you after law school?'" she told the paper. "That's all I could hear over the sound of Marine One. And, wanting to respect protocol, the distance behind the president, kept me from moving closer to hear the question." Zacharia pointed out that it was only her second day on the job. White House press secretary Katie Zacharia looks on as President Trump speaks to reporters on the South Lawn on Oct. 13. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson In a statement to the Washington Post , the White House said that "Katie moved to China with her husband after graduating because of his job at an American private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law." According to USA Today , Zacharia "worked for a Chinese law firm's international-practice team on multimillion-dollar shareholder agreements involving investments through the World Bank." She did not attempt to take the bar exam a second time. On Thursday, Zacharia confirmed that she did not pass the bar, telling the conservative outlet Real America's Voice that she was "incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited" at the time by her impending marriage and move to China. "We just said… 'I'll take the bar and see what happens,'" Zacharia recalled. "The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn't need the bar in China." On Wednesday, a nonprofit watchdog group called Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the California bar asking it to investigate whether Zacharia had violated state law by "repeatedly holding herself out as a lawyer." White House spokesperson Steven Cheung responded on social media by dismissing the Campaign for Accountability as a "radical leftist-organization run by rabid numbskulls suffering from a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome." Legal experts told the Times that it's debatable whether a law school graduate can describe herself as a "lawyer" before she passes the bar. But she cannot call herself an "attorney" — someone who is licensed to practice law and give legal advice — nor can she serve as a "general counsel" or as an "associate" at a Chinese law firm, they added. Zacharia told Real America's Voice that she was "very careful about how I executed this and I never came across as somebody who was an attorney-at-law." "I consulted for a very long time many people in the field — 'Is it OK and acceptable if I label myself 'lawyer' … and provide legal analysis, not legal advice," she explained. "They said, 'Absolutely,' across the board. 'You can call yourself a lawyer.'" On Thursday night, Fox News host Sean Hannity pressed Zacharia on her halting explanation . "Why not just say, 'I went to Pepperdine Law School and then took a different career path, and I took the bar once and didn't pass it'?" Hannity asked. "Why get into this long drawn-out thing about the difference between a lawyer and an attorney?" "When I moved back to the United States, I didn't retake the bar," Zacharia said. "I had four kids in six years. It was never my intent to go into the practice of law." Hours before she was forced out, Zacharia told “Fox & Friends” on Friday that no one had asked whether she passed the bar before she was hired. “Those questions weren’t asked,” she said. “I’m being hired as White House press secretary, not White House counsel,” according to The Hill . What happened in Zacharia's first briefing? White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks with reporters in the Briefing Room on Oct. 13. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson Zacharia's first briefing lasted 15 minutes, most of which was taken up by her opening statement. "I am so honored to work for President Trump and the American people as the new White House press secretary," Zacharia told reporters in the Briefing Room. "I want to thank President Trump for his trust that he has placed in me. I have wanted to work with him for a very long time." She took questions from three news outlets — Breitbart, Fox News and the Daily Mail — before ending the briefing. Asked what she planned to do as press secretary, Zacharia said, "I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was getting to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump's incredible agenda for the American people." In his post on Truth Social announcing her appointment, Trump said Zacharia "has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning." Zacharia called the appointment "the honor of a lifetime" in a post on X . Who is Katie Zacharia? President Donald Trump and Katie Zacharia. Katie Zacharia/X The 42-year-old California native and mother of four left her role as senior communications adviser to Trump Media and Technology Group, which runs Truth Social, to join the White House. Before that, she served for about two months as a deputy assistant secretary and spokesperson for former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, according to her LinkedIn profile . She was best known for her frequent appearances defending the administration's policies on Fox News, CNN, Newsmax, One America News and other outlets. She told CNN in April — around the time she left DHS — that she's a "huge fan of ICE and a big fan of the Border Patrol." Zacharia first came to Washington in 2006 to intern for the Republican National Committee while George W. Bush was president. She lives in California with her husband and their four young children. During Tuesday's briefing, she was asked about juggling the competing roles of being a mother and White House press secretary. "The idea of not spending evenings with my kids is completely unacceptable," Zacharia said, before confusing her spouse with her boss. "So my president — excuse me, my husband — is out here." Zacharia then praised Trump as the "most family-friendly president we've ever had" and said her family will be moving from California to Washington, D.C., soon. CNN reported on Friday that Zacharia's "selection came about quickly" and that she "was not being considered for the role" as of "last week." CNN also reported that "on multiple occasions, senior officials had narrowed down the list" of possible press secretaries "only to find that candidates had said something negative about the president, disqualifying them from the position." In a New York Post column in February , Zacharia recounted a clash with liberal patrons of her "local cardio kickboxing gym" that ended with the gym owner asking her not to wear her red "Team Trump 2024" hat to exercise class. "I responded that I would never take my Trump hat off to appease the left," Zacharia wrote. "I refuse to stay silent." item.title: An armed dad and a teacher stopped an Oregon school shooter. It took just 3 minutes.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Community members grieve at the site of a makeshift memorial in front of Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, on October 16. - Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty Images On a sunny Oregon fall morning, parents dressed their children up and sent them to Silver Rail Elementary School for picture day. It’s the kind of picture parents return to years later, marveling at how small their children once were and how their smiles looked before their faces changed. But for some families, snapshots in their minds from that morning will carry a devastating, final memory of a child who never came home. Just hours after Steven and Angela Nuchols sent their 8-year-old daughter to school, they raced back to Silver Rail, desperate to know whether she was alive, they told local news outlet , The Bend Source . “It was crawling with police officers from all over the county,” Angela Nuchols told The Bend Source . “You’ve got guys in tactical gear, rifles. You’re just scared to death wondering, is your child OK?” For the Nuchols family, the next few hours before they were reunited with their daughter at a church were “the worst three hours of our lives,” Angela said. unknown content item - American schools have repeatedly seen the illusion of safety shattered within the walls of their classrooms. An elementary school in Bend, Oregon, was the latest among them, when a 16-year-old opened fire on Thursday, killing three children, including Rhoam Summer, aged 5; and two others, aged 8 and 11; as well as a 25-year-old teacher, Megan Lambert, police said. A 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were injured and taken to local hospitals, according to officials. When Gretchen Miller learned there was an active shooter at Silver Rail Elementary School, she called her husband and sprinted the block from their home to the school, where their son was inside. Ring camera video captured Miller racing down the street, frantically screaming, “There’s an active shooter at Silver Rail. Oh my God, oh my God, oh my God.” Another school turned into a crime scene; a violation of the sanctity of childhood. A drone view shows Silver Rail Elementary School, the day after a shooting, in Bend, Oregon, October 16. - David Ryder/Reuters 180 seconds of terror Michelle was a freshman in high school in California when she survived a school shooting in 2001. The trauma followed her into adulthood; she learned to scan rooms for exits, sit facing doors and live with anxiety and panic attacks. Long before the shooting, every school drop-off carried a quiet dread. Michelle, who is withholding her last name for privacy, would watch her children go, a pit in her stomach, wondering whether she would see them again. Then, on Thursday, her fifth-grade son called from Silver Rail Elementary School. “Mom, there’s a shooter.” Michelle was eating at an Olive Garden when her son’s voice came through his Apple Watch. She cried while recounting the moment, and said she immediately knew from the sound of his voice that something was terribly wrong. She told him she loved him, urged him to stay quiet and hung up to call 911. As she ran to her car, the call rang without an answer. She raced toward the school, about 10 minutes away. “I was like, how can this happen?” Michelle wonders, her voice shaking. “How can lightning strike twice?” A mother who lived through a 2001 school shooting comforts her son during Silver Rail Elementary shooting. - Michelle The first 911 call came at 12:59 p.m., after the driver of a red pickup truck saw a man approach the school, throw his long gun over the fence and climb over after it, police said Friday. When the pickup driver confronted him, the suspect opened fire, striking the truck at least three times. From her classroom window, fifth-grade teacher Kathy Sheil Smith watched the gunman walk toward the building. She called the main office, then pulled her students into a corner. “They were so afraid. The looks on their faces, it was really hard to see,” Sheil Smith told CNN affiliate KPTV, trying to hold back tears. “Some kids were praying, some kids were consoling other kids. But they were doing so quietly because they know you don’t make any noise.” She wondered whether she would live to see the end of the day. What mattered to her was that her students would. “I’m sure that every teacher at the school thought, ‘Today is the day that I am going to die,’” Sheil Smith told CNN affiliate KPTV . “Save my kids.” As Smith tried to shield her students inside the school, a terrifying picture was emerging. Around 12:59 p.m., emergency dispatchers received a flood of calls reporting that a person had entered the Silver Rail Elementary School and started shooting, according to Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz. At 1:01 p.m., police directed the school to go into lockdown. “Ms. Hawkins, the principal, was saying ‘lockdown, lockdown,’ and then the shots kept on going and going,” one 9-year-old student told CNN affiliate KGW , describing how he hid under a sink for 30 minutes, fearing the gunman would approach his classroom next. “I’m pretty sure a girl. She was saying, ‘Please, please, no,’ and then it was a shot and then dead silence,” he added. The gunman went directly into the classroom just left of the entrance and fired as many as 15 rounds, according to Krantz. The classroom was dedicated to special needs students, according to Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook. A second driver, a 36-year-old father whose children attend the school, had witnessed the initial shooting, drove into the school parking lot and followed the suspect into the school with his legally secured 40-caliber pistol, police said. The bystander was identified by his family as Kaylub Giamanco on Friday. A drone view shows a vehicle belonging to Kaylub Giamanco, the bystander who fatally shot the suspect, in a cordoned-off area at Silver Rail Elementary School, the day after a shooting, in Bend, Oregon, October 16. - David Ryder/Reuters A teacher — who was not injured — threw her cellphone at the shooter and tackled him in an attempt to get the gun away from him, the police chief said. When Giamanco heard gunfire and saw the teacher physically struggling with the gunman, Giamanco entered the classroom and fired, striking the suspect multiple times and killing him, police said. Less than half a mile away, business owner Sierra Jordan told CNN the familiar sound of children laughing and playing outside at recess gave way to the frantic arrival of ambulances. About three minutes after the first 911 call, it was over: At 1:02 p.m., police arrived and reported the shooter had been shot and killed by Giamanco. President Donald Trump called Giamanco “a great hero” who “took care of business.” A photo of Kaylub Giamanco - Kaylub Giamanco/Facebook “Had this not happened, had the bystander not neutralized the shooter? This could have been a much more tragic event than it was,” former FBI special agent Ken Gray told CNN. The shooter was identified as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, a former special needs student at the school, Krantz said Friday. A Maverick 88 pump-action, 12-gauge shotgun was found near the suspect, who had about 44 remaining rounds of 12-gauge ammunition, Krantz added. The gun had been purchased by his mother, a senior law enforcement official briefed on the investigation told CNN earlier Friday. Tragedy plunges community into grief Bend, a picturesque city of about 100,000 people, sits in the high desert landscape of central Oregon. It is a city of sage-scented air, snow-capped peaks and the Deschutes River that cuts through the heart of downtown; a magnet for thrill-seekers finding solace in the nearby mountain trails, red rock cliffs and star-filled skies. Although the city has boomed in recent years, it remains a quiet corner of the American West where the wilderness begins just beyond the city streets and its brick front stores and breweries. “Bend is a place that people move to from bigger cities,” Former Bend Mayor Jeff Eager told CNN . “They move here because it’s relatively safe here; they move here because we have schools you can walk your kids to,” Eager said. “You can’t imagine that it happens here.” But against Bend’s picturesque backdrop, the aftermath looked devastatingly familiar. Parents rushing to a reunification center, hearts clenched with the hope of finding their children among the survivors. Police tape cordoned off the school as officers stood guard. An emergency worker holds up police tape at the scene of a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, October 15. - Rob Kerr/Reuters The minutes had passed so quickly for the rest of the world, but for the families waiting to learn whether their children were alive, the abrupt end of the gunfire wasn’t the end of their agony. The prevalence of school shootings in America should prompt a conversation about “responsible gun ownership,” Democratic Rep. Janelle Bynum of Oregon told CNN. “This school, we had invested money in to make sure that it was locked. They did all of their drills as expected — everything that we’ve said that will protect kids up to now, and yet it didn’t work,” she said. “The laws don’t go far enough, fast enough for us to be able to intervene,” Bynum said. “We have to stop allowing our children to be shredded in schools, grocery stores, parks, churches. We have to stop this violence.” Investigators seek answers The Bend-La Pine school district — of which Silver Rail Elementary School is part — has multiple security measures in place such as secure entry vestibules, photo ID checks and visitor screenings, indoor and outdoor security cameras and upgraded locks on classroom doors that can be secured from inside, according to the district. Despite those measures, some of which were upgraded in 2022, the gunman was able to force his way into the elementary school by shooting at locked doors. It is not yet clear why the shooter was able to bypass security measures, the district’s superintendent said. Investigators are still working to establish a motive for the shooting, authorities said Friday. A search warrant was executed at the alleged shooter’s house on Thursday, according to a senior law enforcement official, who told CNN c omputers and other electronics were taken. Search warrants have also been obtained to gain access to the devices and extract data, according to the source. Local law enforcement and the FBI will examine the material for evidence that could help explain what led to the shooting. The shooter’s parents were cooperative and told investigators their son had attended Silver Rail Elementary School during their interview, the source said. During the pandemic, the shooter’s mother spoke with CNN affiliate KTVZ about her hopes that in-person classes would resume for children with special needs. The program was described as serving children with “intensive behavioral and social skills challenges.” She spoke briefly with CNN off camera from her balcony on Friday but declined to comment on how her son got access to the weapon. Authorities say that is still under investigation. The woman told CNN there were no warning signs. “I miss my boy. I’m so sorry,” the woman said as she cried and smoked a cigarette. In a message to the families of those killed, she said: “I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something. I’m sorry for their loss.” Another chorus of thoughts and prayers Members of the Bend community gathered downtown in Drake Park on Thursday evening for a prayer vigil to support each other and grieve. Bend Mayor Melanie Kebler spoke while in tears alongside Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek, who was also crying. A large crowd of mourners held candles and hugged one another as they listened to prayers, music and community leaders. People wrote tributes in chalk. “NEVER again,” one person wrote. “Be at peace,” scribbled another. A young child knelt to place a lit candle on a step. By Friday, a makeshift memorial had taken shape outside Silver Rail Elementary School. Bouquets of flowers, toys and red, heart-shaped balloons lined a nearby crosswalk, just beyond yellow police tape. One mother, Ally Land, brought her children, 8 and 5, to the memorial. Her children don’t attend Silver Rail, but Land said she wanted to help them understand what had happened, answering their questions as best she could. “I asked them what they knew, and they just said, ‘I know that school’s canceled, so that they can make school safer tomorrow,’” Land told CNN . “We told them something terrible had happened, and we just followed their questions from there.” All Bend-La Pine Schools were closed on Friday, including activities and athletic events, the district said. But a day without classes cannot prevent the next shooting. The Silver Rail Elementary tragedy is the 36th shooting in the United States this year on K-12 school grounds, according to CNN’s analysis of multiple databases, including the Gun Violence Archive. “As a country, we still lack the courage to do anything to try to prevent these things from occurring,” CNN’s Senior Law Enforcement Analyst Charles Ramsey told CNN’s Elex Michaelson on Friday. “And it’s going to happen again.” Blake and Danielle Brinker were at their home outside Bend with Blake’s mother when they learned of the shooting, they told CNN. Blake said, describing his emotions at the time, as “just absolutely gutted.” The pair, who know people directly affected by the shooting, also visited the memorial. “Immediately could feel the energy of the community just stop on a dime,” Blake said. Danielle described Bend as “a very magical place.” A woman lights a candle during a candlelight vigil at Drake Park for victims of the Silver Rail Elementary School shooting, in Bend, Oregon, October 15. - David Ryder/Reuters The town was named in the top 75 safest midsize cities in the country, according to a SmartAsset study earlier this year. But Thursday’s deadly shooting isn’t the first in Bend. In 2022, a 20-year-old gunman, a Bend resident, killed two people after walking into a grocery store with an AR-15-style rifle and opening fire. Back in Bend, Cook, the district superintendent at Bend-La Pine Schools, spent Friday with staff at the school who are grappling with the devastating aftermath. “They are in so much pain, as we all are,” Cook said. “This has been a terrifying and traumatic experience that will affect us all profoundly for years to come.” Michelle, the 2001 school shooting survivor and a mother of children at Silver Rail Elementary School, carried for years the knowledge that gun violence could shatter an ordinary day without warning. But she’d hoped her children would never have to know what that’s like. “My friend said to me, this is generational trauma, this is a second generation that’s been through school shooting trauma,” Michelle told CNN. “How sick is that?” CNN’s Taylor Galgano, Helen Regan, Emma Tucker, Norma Galeana, Caroll Alvarado, Alisha Ebrahimji, Amanda Jackson, Leigh Waldman, John Miller, Rebekah Riess, Elise Hammond and Yan Kaner contributed to this report. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/17/us/bend-oregon-school-shooting-how-it-unfolded

item.title: FEMA lays groundwork to shift disaster burden to states
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Trump administration plans to reduce state and local dependency on federal disaster aid and could move Federal Emergency Management Agency workers out of Washington, D.C., according to an internal FEMA memo obtained by POLITICO. FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton wrote in an Oct. 15 memo — confirmed by two people with direct knowledge of it — that the agency will “strengthen state and local emergency management capacity” in an effort to lower reliance on the federal government. “Reducing federal dependency requires partners to build, maintain, and exercise the capabilities needed to manage incidents effectively,” the seven-page memo to agency employees says. In a separate section, the memo says, “FEMA must reduce unnecessary centralization in Washington, D.C.,” and that “regional and field teams are often closest to disaster survivors, state and local officials, emergency managers, and community partners.” The memo is the clearest indication that the administration will follow through on President Donald Trump’s long-stated desire to shift disaster management to states and reduce the federal role in preparation and recovery. It’s also the first indication of Hamilton’s priorities since he became the first permanent FEMA administrator in Trump’s second term in August. A series of acting leaders had run FEMA since January 2025, and their temporary status precluded the agency from making structural changes. Although Trump has called for weakening FEMA since his first week in office, no new policies emerged, creating uncertainty about the future of federal disaster aid. Trump has indirectly discouraged reliance on federal disaster aid by taking far longer than his predecessors — including Trump in his first term — to act on state requests for help after major storms, floods, wildfires and other disasters. Hamilton’s memo echoes recommendations of a Trump-appointed FEMA review panel to build state and local capacity and make it harder for states to qualify for federal disaster aid. The memo also has general language about “eliminating unnecessary steps, reducing administrative burden” and taking other action to expedite and simplify FEMA’s notoriously slow and laborious process of approving aid. Shana Udvardy of the Union of Concerned Scientists said she worries that the memo “seems to promote efficiency and accountability over the welfare of communities.” “When you have a lot of focus on accountability and efficiency, you’re going to have staff losing focus on the bigger picture of resiliency,” said Udvardy, UCS’ senior climate policy resilience analyst. “It’s really hard to know what this is going to look like in practice.” FEMA did not respond to a request for comment on the memo. The agency has limited ability to revise its own policies, which are mostly set by federal law. Congress hasn’t changed FEMA operations significantly since 2018, and congressional leaders have shown little interest in bipartisan legislation to overhaul the agency. Hamilton says in his memo that the objectives he outlined “will guide FEMA’s planning, budgeting, program management, operations, and partner engagement. Each office, region, and program must assess whether its current activities align with these priorities and identify opportunities to improve execution.” This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/16/fema-state-reliance-federal-aid-01124455

item.title: Pope Leo is discharged from hospital, 4 days after undergoing lung cancer surgery
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Pope Leo XIV was released from Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Saturday, four days after undergoing surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung . The pope exited via the hospital's main entrance. A large crowd waiting outside the hospital cheered for him. He shook hands with several people, then stopped to talk with a young woman who appeared to be wearing a bandage on her right arm and was holding a doll in the image of Pope Leo. The Pope was smiling. Once in the car, he waved to the crowd. His motorcade returned to Vatican City at 3:43 p.m. local time. The 71-year-old pope had a portion of his right lung removed and received a diagnosis of lung cancer earlier this week. No information about his prognosis has been publicly shared. Leo was initially expected to remain hospitalized until Oct. 20 but on Thursday he resumed some work activity , and doctors said Friday that tests confirmed "steady improvement in his recovery." On Saturday morning, the Vatican announced he would leave later in the afternoon. His personal physician and surgeon said in a separate statement that Leo was "deemed fit for discharge from the hospital" based on blood test results and a chest X-ray performed Saturday morning along with an assessment of his clinical condition. The Vatican also confirmed that Leo will recite the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment on Sunday. The pontiff's surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said in an interview with Vatican News that there is no clinical reason the Pope should skip an upcoming trip to South America. The visit, planned for early November, has been in question since Leo's hospitalization. On Friday, the Vatican published the names of journalists accredited to fly on the papal plane to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, signalling that the trip appeared to be going ahead. Leo also conducted some work from the hospital. The Vatican released pictures of the American-born pope standing at an altar in green vestments, celebrating Mass at a small chapel in Gemelli Hospital on Friday. The Vatican also said Leo spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone on Friday, during which he "expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky" in Ukraine . The pope also held separate meetings with Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, the dean of the College of Cardinals, and Cardinal Baldassare Reina, the vicar general of the Diocese of Rome. In the interview with Vatican News, Margaritora said the discovery of the pope's lung tumor was "entirely accidental," and that he had no symptoms. The tumor was found at the base of the lung, Margaritora said, but if it had been "a little higher up, it certainly would not have been seen." "The Holy Father falls into the category of people who discover they have lung cancer entirely by chance – not because they are undergoing preventive screening, but because they undergo examinations for other reasons," Margaritora said. item.title: Proposed bill could be the break Hollywood has been waiting for
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The beleaguered U.S. film and TV industry, which has seen significant dollars leave for foreign countries, local production plummet and thousands of jobs vanish, may have some relief on the way. It comes in the form of proposed legislation that has the rare support of lawmakers across the political spectrum. Indeed, President Donald Trump and the actors union SAG-AFTRA have been equally vocal in throwing their weight behind the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, which aims to create a significant tax incentive to bring Hollywood back home. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The bill was introduced in Congress in late September and is now with the House Ways and Means Committee. Given the bipartisan support, it is likely to have a relative glide path on Capitol Hill. “Both parties represent people who work on sets, run catering companies and own hotels,” said Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas), who co-wrote the bill. “Co-sponsors come from California, Georgia, New York, Ohio and Tennessee, and every one of us has heard the same thing at home: The work is going overseas.” For film and TV creatives and craftspeople, the bill can’t land on the White House’s Resolute Desk a moment too soon. “Whatever you think about the current administration, at least Trump, if he puts his weight behind this, could actually make this really move quickly, which is what we need,” said Carolina Groppa, an Emmy-nominated producer who also hosts a podcast, “Angle on Producers,” about the industry. “The patient’s been on the gurney for a long time, collectively across the United States.” Film and TV production has indeed been fleeing Los Angeles for years - and often leaving the U.S. entirely. Other countries, from Ireland and Canada to Serbia and Colombia, have introduced huge tax incentives that have enticed producers to move projects to wherever is best for the bottom line. According to a recent report from EY Quantitative Economics and Statistics, the share of production spending for studio films with primarily U.S.-based projects declined since the turn of the century from 74 percent to 42 percent; for TV, it fell from 94 percent to 64 percent. That trend accelerated following the 2023 SAG-AFTRA and Writers Guild of America strikes, which were themselves triggered in part by industry contraction following the pandemic. “You could just feel the town change,” said Elsbeth Mumm, a set decorator based in Los Angeles. “Shows were being canceled, movies were getting pushed, scripts were just disappearing, things that had gotten green-lit were just stopped.” The people who have been hurt most are the middle class of the entertainment industry: the writers, production staff and craftspeople who often live project to project. When filmmaking fled overseas, many of their lives changed. “People are losing houses,” Mumm said. “People have lost their health care. People have lost their retirement.” The federal program would give certain film and TV productions a 20 percent tax rebate. To qualify, they would have to cost over $1 million, with at least 75 percent of the principal photography days occurring domestically. The bill would allow the federal rebate to be stacked on top of existing state incentives. “If what is in the bill goes through and is executed as promised, it will be a massive game changer,” said Patrick Meaney, an independent film director. “I think people are almost underrating it or not really processing it because it came out of nowhere and seems too good to be true.” The tax incentive structure is somewhat similar to a smaller plan in effect in California, which last year was significantly broadened to include up to $750 million in credits annually. Many in Hollywood feel the program’s expansion has been a success. The outlook is hopeful “for the first time in a long time,” said Keith Raskin, a veteran producer currently working on a crime comedy, “Sunset P.I.,” which is set to premiere on NBC in 2027. He’s filming in Los Angeles thanks to the state tax rebate program. “When I make phone calls to crew members to hire them, they cry because it means that they can make a payment on their house or they can keep their insurance for another year.” If the federal rebate passes, it would mean “we’re finally a player in the world market,” Raskin added. One big difference from the California credit: The federal version is uncapped. Despite its bipartisan support, some critics argue that the tax incentives would first and foremost benefit the richest players in the system - massive entities like Paramount Skydance and the star actors and directors who are their top moneymakers. “Do we really need kickbacks to corporations to employ a whole labor force?” asked Andi Brittan, a veteran set decorator and union leader at the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees Local 44. “Unfortunately, the truth is, we have to work within the system, and working within the system means supporting these kinds of tax incentives.” Other detractors point to past economic reports showing that these kinds of tax subsidies provide little to no quantifiable value. For example, a 2023 report published by the state of New York found that from 2012 to 2022, the tax incentives didn’t generate as many jobs as would have been created in other industries. Still, the report also noted there are probably indirect positive economic effects that are hard to quantify. That’s something many in the industry focus on. “It’s not just the films,” Mumm said. “It’s the trickling out - the florists, the food stylists, all of this stuff outside of the industry that rely on this huge force purchasing from them.” It may be too late to ever fully recover from years of being beat on production costs, and there’s still major concern about the impact of the Paramount Skydance acquisition of Warner Bros. Even so, the rank and file of the U.S. film industry are uttering words like “optimistic.” “I feel a good amount of hope, and I’ll tell you why,” said Kevin Armento, a film and TV writer. “All those soundstages are still sitting there. They haven’t bulldozed them yet.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/business/2026/10/17/tax-breaks-tinseltown-would-aim-keep-film-tv-production-us/
